extracted.intended_audience: Informed citizens and delegates evaluating the proposed U.S. Constitution (readers of the Federalist Papers)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether the proposed number, selection, and safeguards for the House of Representatives are sufficient to protect public liberty and represent constituents' interests under the new federal Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of Representatives (initial and per-population rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of which this branch of the legislature is to consist, at the outset of the government, will be sixty-five; within three years a census is to be taken, when the number may be augmented to one for every thirty thousand inhabitants; and within every successive period of ten years the census is to be renewed, and augmentations may continue to be made under the above limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This temporary smallness is defensible because the Constitution provides for census-based reapportionment (one per 30,000 max) and regular augmentation; projections (accounting for population growth and three-fifths rule) indicate the House will grow to 100, 200, then 400 over decades, removing fears about initial small size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of Representatives' Knowledge for Federal Objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The representative ought to be acquainted with the interests and circumstances of his constituents only insofar as those circumstances relate to the objects within the purview of federal authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal objects are primarily commerce, taxation, and the militia. Much local detail relevant to these can be conveyed by a few knowledgeable representatives, by state laws/codes, and by having reps who are or have been state legislators; thus a moderate number of reps can possess requisite information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal Safety of Small Representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether sixty-five members for a few years, and a hundred or two hundred for a few more, be a safe depositary for a limited and well-guarded power of legislating for the United States?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate this by: the current 'genius' and spirit of the American people, the monitoring capability of State legislatures, the improbability that so few men would form a conspiracy of tyranny within short two-year terms, and historical experience (e.g., the Revolutionary Congress) showing public councils were not betrayed despite temptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent Elections and Short Terms as a Restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Such a limitation of the term of appointments as will maintain a proper responsibility to the people; frequent elections keep representatives mindful of dependence on constituents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-year terms ensure members anticipate their power ceasing and being reviewed frequently, providing a habitual recollection of dependence and making betrayal or ambition less probable; frequent elections are among the most effectual means republican government uses to prevent degeneracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on Accepting Offices that Arise During Term
rubrics_metrics.description: The members of the Congress are rendered ineligible to any civil offices that may be created, or of which the emoluments may be increased, during the term of their election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because no offices with newly-created or increased emoluments can be distributed to sitting members (only ordinary vacancies), the yield of appointments is limited and cannot reasonably be expected to purchase the guardians of the people; this reduces danger from executive dispensation of appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad Electoral Franchise and Equality of Eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Who are to be the electors of the federal representatives? The electors are to be the great body of the people of the United States. Who are to be the objects of popular choice? Every citizen whose merit may recommend him—no qualification of wealth, of birth, of religious faith, or of civil profession is permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess representation quality by whether elections are open to the general body of people and eligibility is unrestricted by wealth or birth; larger electorates (thousands) are argued to be as capable or more so in choosing fit representatives than smaller electorates (hundreds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity—Legislation Applies to Legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: They can make no law which will not have its full operation on themselves and their friends, as well as on the great mass of the society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mutual applicability of laws is a strong bond connecting rulers and people and is a safeguard against self-serving legal discriminations; judges of representation should weigh this structural constraint when assessing risk of legislative abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative Experience (British House of Commons) as Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of inhabitants in England and Scotland is about eight millions, with 558 representatives in the House of Commons — roughly one representative per thirty thousand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative historical evidence: despite imperfections, Britain preserved a 'valuable portion of freedom' with similar representative ratios, suggesting one per 30,000 in the U.S. will be a 'safe and competent guardian' of entrusted interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional Mechanisms and Political Incentives for Augmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Within every successive term of ten years a census of inhabitants is to be repeated... to readjust apportionment and to augment the number of representatives under the sole limitation that the whole number shall not exceed one for every thirty thousand inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether augmentation will occur by noting: (1) the explicit decennial census and reapportionment rule; (2) that larger states will politically favor increases; (3) the House's control of the purse gives leverage; and (4) senators from growing new states will support reapportionment — together these provide strong practical assurance of augmentation as population demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Knowledge Not Always Necessary for Federal Regulation (especially militia)
rubrics_metrics.description: With regard to the regulation of the militia, there are scarcely any circumstances in reference to which local knowledge can be said to be necessary... The art of war teaches general principles of organization, movement, and discipline, which apply universally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For subjects like militia regulation (and much commerce regulation), general principles and the 'face of the country' (mountainous vs. level) suffice; therefore, lack of extremely detailed local knowledge does not make representation incompetent for these federal objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improbability of Corruption by Foreign Gold or Executive Influence
rubrics_metrics.description: If foreign gold could so easily corrupt our federal rulers... The only means [to corrupt] will be in the dispensation of appointments... their emoluments of office ... will not, and without a previous corruption of the House of Representatives cannot, more than suffice for very different purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess corruption risk by considering: limited emoluments, the ineligibility rule for offices during a term, oversight by State legislatures, and historical precedents (e.g., conduct of the Revolutionary Congress), all of which make wholesale bribery or executive subjugation unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffusive Mode of Election Does Not Necessarily Elevate an Oligarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: The objection that diffusive modes of choosing representatives (larger electorates) tend to elevate the few at the expense of the many is erroneous; larger electorates (5–6k voters) are not less capable of choosing fit representatives than smaller electorates (hundreds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use domestic examples: senatorial districts, state assemblies, and executive councils elected by large bodies show no trend to elevate traitors or undermine liberty; reason suggests larger electorates are more likely to select fit representatives and resist corruption or intrigue.
